Chapter 7: Statistical Power

STA258: Statistics with Applied Probability
University of Toronto Mississauga

Nishan Mudalige, Sarah Halime, Ashwin Selvapandian

Chapter Roadmap

7.1 - Power

What power means, and the four things that push it up or down.

7.2 - Errors

Type I (\(\alpha\)) and Type II (\(\beta\)), and how power \(=1-\beta\).

7.3 - Planning

Use a target power to choose the smallest sample size.


Core skill

Compute power against a specific alternative value.

Core tool

Use pnorm() and qnorm() for cutoffs, power, and sample size.

Core habit

A test is only useful if it can detect a real effect.

7.1 What Is Statistical Power?

Definition 7.1 The probability that a fixed-level significance test will reject \(H_0\) when a particular alternative value of the parameter is true is called the power of the test against that alternative.

\[\text{Power at }\theta=\theta_a =P(\text{reject }H_0\mid \theta=\theta_a), \qquad 0\le \text{power}\le 1\]

High power (near 1) The test is good at detecting effects that are really there.

Low power (near 0) The test has a high chance of failing to detect the specific alternative effect being considered.

Question

The power of a hypothesis test is the probability that the test will:

  • Reject \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is actually true
  • Reject \(H_0\) when \(H_a\) is actually true
  • Fail to reject \(H_0\) when \(H_a\) is true
  • Fail to reject \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is true

What Affects Power?

1. Effect size  -  Larger gaps between reality and \(H_0\) are easier to detect \(\Rightarrow\) more power.

2. Sample size \(n\)  -  Larger samples shrink the standard error \(\Rightarrow\) more power.

3. Significance level \(\alpha\)  -  A larger \(\alpha\) makes \(H_0\) easier to reject \(\Rightarrow\) more power (but more Type I risk).

4. Variability \(\sigma\)  -  Less spread in the data \(\Rightarrow\) narrower sampling distribution \(\Rightarrow\) more power.

Researchers choose \(n\), \(\alpha\), and the smallest effect worth detecting. Variability is usually estimated from prior information, so sample size is often the main planning lever.

Question

Holding the effect size, \(\sigma\), and \(n\) fixed, you raise the significance level from \(\alpha=0.01\) to \(\alpha=0.05\). What happens to the power?

  • Power decreases
  • Power increases
  • Power is unchanged
  • Power always becomes exactly 1

7.2 Type I and Type II Errors

A hypothesis test can reach the wrong conclusion in two ways.

\(H_0\) True \(H_0\) False
Reject \(H_0\) Type I (\(\alpha\)) Correct (power)
Fail to reject \(H_0\) Correct Type II (\(\beta\))

Type I error (\(\alpha\)) Reject \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is true.

Type II error (\(\beta\)) Fail to reject \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is false.

The consequences of Type I and Type II errors depend on the context. We choose \(\alpha\) in advance to control the probability of a Type I error when \(H_0\) is true.

Power Connects to the Errors

The power of a test against an alternative is 1 minus the Type II error probability for that alternative:

\[\text{Power}=1-\beta = 1 - P(\text{Type II})\]

Reading the picture The orange tail under \(H_0\) is \(\alpha\). The red region under \(H_a\) is \(\beta\). Everything else under \(H_a\) is the power.

Question

A test fails to reject \(H_0\), but in reality \(H_0\) is false. Which error has occurred?

  • Type I error
  • Type II error
  • No error, we were cautious
  • Both Type I and Type II

Computing Power: The Recipe

  1. 1. Rejection rule in terms of the estimate. Convert the critical \(z\) (or \(z_\alpha\)) into a cutoff \(\bar{x}_*\) on the data scale using the null distribution.
  2. 2. Switch to the alternative. Assume the alternative value of the parameter is true.
  3. 3. Compute the rejection probability. Standardize the cutoff under the alternative and read off the area, which is the power.

Example: A Better Espresso Blend

A specialty coffee roaster’s house espresso has scored a long-run average of 7.0 on a 10-point flavour scale. A new blend is developed, and the roaster will switch only if it truly scores higher. If the new blend’s true mean score is \(\mu=8.1\), will a 5% test reliably detect the improvement?

A panel of \(n=10\) trained graders scores the new blend; from years of calibration, grader scores have \(\sigma=1\).

\(\sigma\) is known \(\Rightarrow\) one-sample \(z\) test with reference distribution \(N(0,1)\).

Set-up

\[H_0:\mu = 7 \qquad H_a:\mu>7\]

  • \(n = 10,\quad \sigma = 1,\quad \alpha = 0.05\)
  • Detect the alternative \(\mu = 8.1\)

Espresso: Cutoff to Power

Rejection Rule One-sided \(\alpha=0.05\) gives \(z_{\text{crit}}=1.645\). On the \(\bar{x}\) scale (since \(\sigma\) is known): \[\bar{x}_*=7+1.645\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\approx 7.520 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{reject if } \bar{x}>7.520\]

Find the Power Assume \(\mu=8.1\) is true and find \(P(\bar{x}>7.520)\): \[\text{power}=P\!\left(Z>\tfrac{7.520-8.1}{1/\sqrt{10}}\right)=P(Z>-1.83)=\mathbf{0.9664}\]

A 96.6% chance of correctly detecting \(\mu=8.1\). Since power \(=1-\beta\), the green and red areas add to 1: \[\text{power}=1-\beta=1-0.034=0.966\]

Check in R: Espresso Power

Visualizing Power: The Power Curve

Power is not a single number, it is a function of the true mean. Plotting power against \(\mu\) gives the power curve.

Read it like this

  • At \(\mu=\mu_0\), power equals \(\alpha\).
  • As the true \(\mu\) moves farther above \(\mu_0\) in the direction of \(H_a\), power climbs toward 1.
  • The orange dots mark \(\mu=7.52\) (power \(\approx 0.5\)) and \(\mu=8.1\) (power \(\approx 0.97\)).

Question

On the power curve for a one-sided test, what happens to the power as the true mean moves farther away from the null value (in the direction of \(H_a\))?

  • It decreases toward \(0\)
  • It increases toward \(1\)
  • It stays constant at \(\alpha\)
  • It is always equal to \(\beta\)

Example: Under-Dosed Medicine Vials

A pharmaceutical filling machine should dispense \(\mu_0=300\) mg of active drug per vial, with known \(\sigma=3\) mg from the validated assay. A routine quality check tests only \(n=6\) vials — will a 5% test catch a machine that has drifted to a true mean of \(\mu=299\) mg? \[H_0:\mu = 300 \qquad H_a:\mu<300 \qquad (\alpha=0.05)\]

\[\bar{x}_*=300-1.645\cdot\tfrac{3}{\sqrt6}=297.985 \quad(\text{reject if } \bar{x}<297.985)\] \[\text{power}=P\!\left(Z<\frac{297.985-299}{3/\sqrt6}\right)=P(Z<-0.83)=\mathbf{0.2033}\]

Only 20% power. With just 6 vials, this check will usually miss an under-dosing machine — the sample is too small.

Check in R: Vial Power

Try bumping n to 30 or 60 and re-run, then watch the power climb as the standard error shrinks.

Interactive: Watch Power Climb with \(n\)

Use the dropdown to change the sample size for the vial check (\(\mu_0=300\), \(\mu_a=299\), \(\sigma=3\), left-tailed \(\alpha=0.05\)). As \(n\) grows, both curves sharpen, they separate more cleanly, and the green power area past the cutoff expands.

Same 1 mg shortfall, same \(\alpha\), only \(n\) changes: power rises from \(\approx 0.20\) at \(n=6\) to \(\approx 0.83\) at \(n=60\). That is why sample size is your main planning lever.

Interactive: Change Everything

Choose the direction of \(H_a\), then drag \(\mu_0\), \(\mu_a\), \(\sigma\), and \(n\) (\(\alpha\) stays at \(0.05\)) and watch the cutoff, \(\beta\), and power react.

viewof alt = Inputs.select(
  new Map([["μ > μ₀ (greater)", "greater"],
           ["μ < μ₀ (less)", "less"],
           ["μ ≠ μ₀ (two-sided)", "two.sided"]]),
  {value: "greater", label: "Hₐ"}
)
viewof mu0 = Inputs.range([5, 15], {value: 10, step: 0.5, label: "μ₀"})
viewof mua = Inputs.range([5, 15], {value: 12, step: 0.5, label: "μₐ"})
viewof sigma = Inputs.range([1, 4], {value: 2, step: 0.5, label: "σ"})
viewof n = Inputs.range([2, 60], {value: 10, step: 1, label: "n"})
res = {
  const pnorm = (z) => {
    const t = 1 / (1 + 0.2316419 * Math.abs(z));
    const d = Math.exp(-z * z / 2) / Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI);
    const p = d * t * (0.319381530 + t * (-0.356563782 + t * (1.781477937 +
              t * (-1.821255978 + t * 1.330274429))));
    return z >= 0 ? 1 - p : p;
  };
  const se = sigma / Math.sqrt(n);
  let cuts, inReject, pow;
  if (alt === "greater") {
    cuts = [mu0 + 1.6449 * se];
    inReject = (x) => x > cuts[0];
    pow = 1 - pnorm((cuts[0] - mua) / se);
  } else if (alt === "less") {
    cuts = [mu0 - 1.6449 * se];
    inReject = (x) => x < cuts[0];
    pow = pnorm((cuts[0] - mua) / se);
  } else {
    cuts = [mu0 - 1.96 * se, mu0 + 1.96 * se];
    inReject = (x) => x < cuts[0] || x > cuts[1];
    pow = pnorm((cuts[0] - mua) / se) + 1 - pnorm((cuts[1] - mua) / se);
  }
  const lo = Math.min(mu0, mua) - 4.2 * se;
  const hi = Math.max(mu0, mua) + 4.2 * se;
  const dnorm = (x, m) => Math.exp(-0.5 * ((x - m) / se) ** 2) / (se * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI));
  const data = d3.range(lo, hi, (hi - lo) / 500).map((x) =>
    ({x, h0: dnorm(x, mu0), ha: dnorm(x, mua)}));
  return {se, cuts, inReject, pow, data};
}

Example: Monitoring a Server Room

A data centre keeps its server hall at \(\mu_0=22\)°C. Too hot and the servers overheat and fail; too cold and the cooling bill climbs for no benefit. Each day the monitoring system samples \(n=16\) sensor readings; from the sensors’ calibration, \(\sigma=2\)°C. If the cooling has truly drifted to \(\mu=23\)°C, how likely is the daily check to flag it?

A shift in either direction matters \(\Rightarrow\) two-sided test: \(\alpha\) splits into two tails of \(\alpha/2=0.025\) each, so \(z_{\alpha/2}=1.96\) and there are two cutoffs.

Set-up

\[H_0:\mu = 22 \qquad H_a:\mu \neq 22\]

  • \(n = 16,\quad \sigma = 2,\quad \alpha = 0.05\)
  • Detect the alternative \(\mu = 23\)
  • \(\sigma\) known \(\Rightarrow\) one-sample \(z\) test

Two-Sided: Two Cutoffs, Two Power Pieces

Rejection Rule Two cutoffs, using \(z_{\alpha/2}=1.96\): \[\bar{x}_*=22 \pm 1.96\cdot\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{16}} = 22 \pm 0.98\] \[\text{reject if } \bar{x}<21.02 \;\text{ or }\; \bar{x}>22.98\]

Find the Power Assume \(\mu=23\) is true; add the two rejection pieces: \[\begin{aligned} \text{power} &= P(\bar{x}<21.02)+P(\bar{x}>22.98)\\ &= P(Z<-3.96)+P(Z>-0.04)\\ &\approx 0.000+0.516=\mathbf{0.516} \end{aligned}\]

Question

A test has low power against the alternative it was designed to detect. Which single change raises power the most without touching \(\alpha\) or the true process?

  • Use a smaller sample to save money
  • Increase the sample size \(n\)
  • Re-label the hypotheses
  • Hope the next sample looks different

7.3 Using Power to Determine Sample Size

Too small Low power - real, meaningful effects are more likely to go undetected because the risk of a Type II error is higher.

Too large Wasteful - extra time, cost, and participants for precision you did not need.

Power analysis finds the minimum \(n\) that detects an effect of a given size with a specified probability (power), while holding the Type I rate at \(\alpha\).

To run it you must supply four ingredients: the standard deviation \(\sigma\), the significance level \(\alpha\), the target power, and the effect-size magnitude \(|\mu_a-\mu_0|\) you want to detect.

The Sample-Size Idea

  1. 1. Cutoff from \(H_0\). The cutoff \(\bar{x}_*\) is the borderline value of the sample mean that decides whether you reject \(H_0\) or not. Write it using the null mean and the critical value \(z_\alpha\).
  2. 2. Cutoff from the target power. Write the same \(\bar{x}_*\) using the alternative mean and \(z_{\text{power}}\), the standard-normal quantile corresponding to the target power.
  3. 3. Set the two expressions equal and solve for \(n\). Round up to the next whole observation.

One-sided sample-size formula

\[ n= \left( \frac{(z_\alpha+z_{\text{power}})\sigma} {|\mu_a-\mu_0|} \right)^2 \]

where \(z_{\text{power}}\) is the standard-normal quantile corresponding to the target power.

Example: Detecting a Lift in Daily Active Minutes

A product team’s app currently averages \(\mu_0=100\) daily active minutes. A new onboarding flow is believed to lift engagement. With \(\sigma=14\), they want power \(0.60\) to detect a true mean of \(\mu=103\). What is the smallest \(n\)? \[H_0:\mu=100 \qquad H_a:\mu>100 \qquad (\alpha=0.05)\]

Cutoff under \(H_0\) \(\;\bar{x}_*=100+1.645\cdot\tfrac{14}{\sqrt n}\)

Cutoff for power 0.60 \(\;P(Z>-0.25)\approx 0.60 \;\Rightarrow\; \bar{x}_*=103-0.25\cdot\tfrac{14}{\sqrt n}\)

Equate and solve \[100+1.645\cdot\tfrac{14}{\sqrt n}=103-0.25\cdot\tfrac{14}{\sqrt n} \;\Rightarrow\; n=\left(\frac{(1.645+0.25)\cdot 14}{103-100}\right)^2\approx 78.2 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{n=79}\]

Check in R: Sample Size for the Lift

Using the full normal quantiles gives \(n\approx 78.47\), so round up to 79 observations to obtain planned power of at least 0.60 under the assumed values of \(\sigma\) and the target effect. Using the rounded value \(z_{\text{power}}=0.25\) gives \(n\approx 78.2\) and the same final answer.

Example: Vending-Machine Coffee

A campus vending machine advertises \(225\) ml cups (\(\sigma=7\) ml). You suspect it pours less. How many cups must you sample to reach power \(0.80\) against a true mean of \(\mu=223\) ml? (Target: \(P(Z<0.84)\approx0.80\), so \(z_{\text{power}}=0.84\).) \[H_0:\mu=225 \qquad H_a:\mu<225 \qquad (\alpha=0.05)\]

Equate the two cutoffs \(\;225-1.645\tfrac{7}{\sqrt n}=223+0.84\tfrac{7}{\sqrt n}\)

Solve for \(n\) \[n=\left(\frac{(1.645+0.84)\cdot 7}{225-223}\right)^2\approx 75.6 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{n=76}\]

Using the full normal quantiles gives \(n\approx 75.74\), so round up to 76 cups to obtain planned power of at least 0.80 against a 2 ml shortfall. The rounded values \(1.645\) and \(0.84\) give \(n\approx 75.6\) and the same final answer.

Check in R: Coffee Sample Size

Because \(\sigma\) is treated as known, this chapter calculates the required sample size directly using standard-normal quantiles. power.t.test() performs power calculations for a t-test, so it does not exactly reproduce this known-\(\sigma\) \(z\)-test calculation.

Power for a Proportion: Same Logic

For a one-sided test of \(p\), the rejection cutoff uses the null standard error, but power is computed with the alternative standard error:

\[\hat p^{\,*}=p_0 \mathbin{\substack{+\\[-4pt]-}} z_\alpha\sqrt{\tfrac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}, \qquad \text{power}=P\!\left(\hat p \text{ in reject region}\;\middle|\; p=p_a\right)\]

Which sign on \(z_\alpha\)?

Test Cutoff \(\hat p^{\,*}\) Reject when
\(H_a:p<p_0\) \(p_0-z_\alpha\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}\) \(\hat p<\hat p^{\,*}\)
\(H_a:p>p_0\) \(p_0+z_\alpha\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}\) \(\hat p>\hat p^{\,*}\)

Three steps, same as the mean

  • Find the cutoff \(\hat p^{\,*}\) from \(p_0\) and \(z_\alpha\).
  • Standardize that cutoff under \(p=p_a\) using \(\text{SE}_a\).
  • The tail area past it is the power.

A Streaming Proportion Test

A streaming platform claims \(90\%\) of viewers finish episode 1. Researchers suspect fewer do, and test \(H_0:p=0.90\) vs \(H_a:p<0.90\) at \(\alpha=0.05\). The truth is \(p=0.85\).

The question How does the power to detect this 5-point drop change as the sample grows from \(n=50\) to \(n=200\)?

Streaming Example: Power Grows with \(n\)

\(n\) cutoff \(\hat p^{\,*}\) \(z\) under \(p=0.85\) Power
50 0.8302 \(-0.39\) 0.347
100 0.8507 \(0.02\) 0.507
200 0.8651 \(0.60\) 0.725

Same effect (a drop from 0.90 to 0.85), same \(\alpha\), only \(n\) changes. Power climbs from 35% to 73%.

Check in R: Proportion Power

How Many Viewers for Power 0.80?

Keep \(H_0:p=0.90\), \(H_a:p<0.90\), true \(p=0.85\), \(\alpha=0.05\). Set power \(=0.80\) (\(z_{1-\beta}=0.8416\)) and equate the two cutoff expressions: \[0.90-1.645\sqrt{\tfrac{0.90(0.10)}{n}}=0.85+0.8416\sqrt{\tfrac{0.85(0.15)}{n}}\]

\[\sqrt n=\frac{1.645\sqrt{0.09}+0.8416\sqrt{0.1275}}{0.05}=\frac{0.4935+0.3005}{0.05}\approx 15.88\] \[n\approx 252.2 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{n=253}\]

Detecting a modest 5-point drop with 80% power takes 253 viewers, far more than the 50-200 above. Smaller effects always demand larger samples.

General Power Formulas

Right-tailed, \(H_a:\mu>\mu_0\) \[\text{Power}(\mu_a)=\pi(\mu_a)=P\!\left[\,Z\ge z_\alpha+\frac{\sqrt n\,(\mu_0-\mu_a)}{\sigma}\right]\]

Left-tailed, \(H_a:\mu<\mu_0\) \[\text{Power}(\mu_a)=\pi(\mu_a)=P\!\left[\,Z\le -z_\alpha+\frac{\sqrt n\,(\mu_0-\mu_a)}{\sigma}\right]\]

Two-sided, \(H_a:\mu\ne\mu_0\) \[\text{Power}(\mu_a)=1-P\!\left[-z_{\alpha/2}+\frac{\sqrt n\,(\mu_0-\mu_a)}{\sigma}\le Z\le z_{\alpha/2}+\frac{\sqrt n\,(\mu_0-\mu_a)}{\sigma}\right]\]

What You Need to Know

Standard deviation

\(\sigma\) = the spread of the variable being measured.

Significance level

\(\alpha\) = the fixed Type I error rate you are willing to tolerate.

Effect size

\(|\mu_a-\mu_0|\) = the magnitude of the smallest difference worth detecting.

Question

You want to detect a smaller effect than originally planned, keeping \(\alpha\), \(\sigma\), and power the same. What happens to the required sample size?

  • It decreases
  • It stays the same
  • It increases
  • It becomes undefined

Power Cheat Sheet

Quantity Formula / idea
Power against \(\theta_a\) \(1-\beta(\theta_a)=P(\text{reject }H_0\mid\theta=\theta_a)\)
Type I error \(\alpha=P(\text{reject }H_0\mid H_0\text{ true})\)
Type II error \(\beta=P(\text{fail to reject }H_0\mid H_0\text{ false})\)
Cutoff (right-tailed) \(\bar{x}_*=\mu_0+z_\alpha\,\sigma/\sqrt{n}\)
Power (right-tailed) \(P\!\left(Z\ge z_\alpha+\sqrt{n}\dfrac{\mu_0-\mu_a}{\sigma}\right)\)
Sample size (one-sided) \(n=\left(\dfrac{(z_\alpha+z_{1-\beta})\sigma}{|\mu_a-\mu_0|}\right)^2\)

Always round a computed sample size up to the next whole observation so the achieved power is at least the target.

Chapter Summary

Power Power is the probability of rejecting \(H_0\) at a specific alternative value, and it equals \(1-\beta\).

What Changes Power Power rises with a larger effect size, larger sample size, or larger \(\alpha\), and falls with greater variability.

Study Planning Choose a meaningful effect and target power, solve for the required sample size, and always round \(n\) up.


One-slide takeaway. A hypothesis test should be planned to have enough power to detect an effect that matters.
